text: Python handles everyday arithmetic with the operators you already know, plus a couple you might not expect from a calculator.
[chuckle] Plus adds, minus subtracts, the star means multiply, and the forward slash divides — nothing surprising yet.
But here's the first twist: a double slash gives you integer division, dividing and then throwing away everything after the decimal point.
The percent sign is modulo, [sniff] which hands you the remainder left over after that division — incredibly useful for checking even or odd numbers.
And a double star raises a number to a power, so ten double-star three is ten cubed, one thousand.
Watch all seven of those operations run on the very same two numbers, and you get seven completely different results.
[groan] Python also ships a set of built-in math functions, so you rarely need to write the basics yourself.
Abs gives the absolute value, stripping away any negative sign, and round lets you control exactly how many decimal places you keep.
Max and min instantly pick out the larger or the smaller of a group of numbers, no comparison code needed.
And just like in math class, Python respects operator precedence — multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, unless you add parentheses to force your own order.
And one final gotcha worth remembering: dividing two whole numbers with a single slash always gives you back a float, [laugh] even when the numbers divide perfectly evenly.
